name: Bank of Credit and Commerce International

summary.text: The Bank of Credit and Commerce International (BCCI) was an international bank founded in 1972 by Pakistani banker Agha Hasan Abedi, with Abu Dhabi's ruling family as founding and majority shareholders. A December 1992 report to the U.S. Senate Foreign Relations Committee by Senators John Kerry and Hank Brown found that BCCI operated in 73 countries through a structure designed to evade regulation. The report documented fraud, money laundering, bribery and support of arms trafficking, and found that the CIA used BCCI and its secretly owned U.S. subsidiary First American for operations. BCCI was closed by regulators on July 5, 1991.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Executive Summary

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI, the CIA and Foreign Intelligence

facts.claim: A December 1992 report to the Senate Foreign Relations Committee by Senators John Kerry and Hank Brown ('The BCCI Affair') concluded that the CIA used BCCI and its secretly held U.S. subsidiary First American for CIA operations even after it knew BCCI was a criminal enterprise. The report also found that the CIA failed to provide the critical information it had gathered on BCCI to the Federal Reserve and the Justice Department.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI, the CIA and Foreign Intelligence

facts.claim: On July 5, 1991, BCCI was closed in a coordinated action by regulators led by the Bank of England, which relied on information from the bank's auditors, Price Waterhouse, about fraud at BCCI.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Executive Summary

facts.claim: The Bank of England's Banking Act report for 1991/92 describes the 5 July 1991 closure as a coordinated worldwide operation by banking supervisors: the Bank obtained a court order appointing provisional liquidators for BCCI SA, the Luxembourg-incorporated bank; similar action was taken in Luxembourg and in Grand Cayman in respect of BCCI Overseas; and supervisors in other jurisdictions where BCCI had subsidiaries or agencies moved to shut those operations. An emergency unit at the Bank, staffed from the Bank and several overseas supervisory authorities, coordinated the action. A winding-up order against BCCI SA was made on 14 January 1992.
facts.quote: The closure was a co-ordinated worldwide operation by banking supervisors. On 5 July, the Bank obtained a Court order for the appointment of provisional liquidators in relation to BCCI SA, the Luxembourg-incorporated bank. Similar action was taken in Luxembourg, and also in Grand Cayman in respect of BCCI Overseas.

sources.publisher: Bank of England
sources.title: Banking Act Report 1991/92

facts.claim: According to the Bank of England's Banking Act report for 1991/92, the closure followed the Bank's receipt of a report from Price Waterhouse commissioned under Section 41 of the Banking Act; the Bank stated that information in that report made it necessary, to protect the interests of existing and potential depositors, to freeze BCCI's assets by closing the institution.
facts.quote: It followed the Bank's receipt of a report from Price Waterhouse commissioned under Section 41 of the Banking Act.

sources.publisher: Bank of England
sources.title: Banking Act Report 1991/92

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report by Senators Kerry and Brown (December 1992) states that Price Waterhouse's June 1991 review of BCCI, which the report calls the 'Sandstorm Report', was the final evidence that led to the global shutdown of BCCI on July 5, 1991, and quotes it as finding that BCCI's accounting records had completely failed, and continued to fail, to meet the standard required of institutions authorised under the UK Banking Act. The report says the Sandstorm Report was provided to the Subcommittee only in a heavily censored form by the Federal Reserve, at the insistence of the Bank of England, which cited British secrecy law.
facts.quote: was the final evidence that lead to the shutdown of BCCI globally on July 5, 1991

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI and its Accountants

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (mirror hosted by GlobalSecurity.org)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI and its Accountants

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) found that by early 1985 the CIA knew more about BCCI's goals and intentions concerning the U.S. banking system than anyone else in government and had reported BCCI's secret purchase of First American by 1985, but that the CIA failed to provide this information to the Federal Reserve and the Justice Department; that the Treasury received it but did not pass it to the Federal Reserve in 1985 and 1986; and that, according to Assistant Attorney General Mueller's testimony, the Justice Department was not on the CIA's dissemination list until 1990. The original 1985 CIA report was lost and has never been located by the CIA.
facts.quote: By early 1985, the CIA knew more about BCCI's goals and intentions concerning the U.S. banking system than anyone else in government.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI, the CIA and Foreign Intelligence

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) stated that the initial information the CIA provided to the Subcommittee was untrue, later information was incomplete, and the Agency resisted providing a full account of its knowledge of BCCI until almost a year after the initial requests; the Subcommittee learned there were hundreds, not two, of CIA memoranda on BCCI disseminated to other agencies. The CIA's witness, Kerr, acknowledged the CIA had used BCCI for certain intelligence-gathering operations and characterized the use as limited and routine, which a Senate Intelligence Committee audit confirmed on that point.
facts.quote: Initial information that was provided by the CIA was untrue; later information that was provided was incomplete; and the Agency resisted providing a "full" account about its knowledge of BCCI until almost a year after the initial requests for the information.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI, the CIA and Foreign Intelligence

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) found that, beginning in late 1977, Clark Clifford and Robert Altman assisted BCCI in purchasing Financial General Bankshares (later First American Bankshares) with the participation of nominees, understanding BCCI's central involvement in directing and controlling the transaction; that key First American decisions were made initially by BCCI and communicated to Clifford and Altman, who secured ratification by First American's boards; and that in 1988 Mohammed Hammoud bought Clifford's and Altman's First American shares with funds lent to him by BCCI.
facts.quote: Beginning in late 1977, Clifford and Altman assisted BCCI in purchasing a U.S. bank, Financial General Bankshares, with the participation of nominees, and understood BCCI's central involvement in directing and controlling the transaction.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Executive Summary

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI in the United States - Part Two: Acquisition, Consolidation, and Consequences

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Mohammed Hammoud: BCCI's Flexible Front-Man

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) found that the Bank of England withheld important information from the Federal Reserve in the spring of 1990 about the size and scope of BCCI's lending on CCAH/First American shares, which delayed the opening of a full Federal Reserve investigation by approximately eight months, and concluded that BCCI's British auditors, Abu Dhabi owners and British regulators had become BCCI's partners 'not in crime, but in cover-up'.
facts.quote: BCCI's British auditors, Abu Dhabi owners, and British regulators, had now become BCCI's partners, not in crime, but in cover-up

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: The Regulators

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) found that the Federal Reserve approved the 1981 CCAH takeover of Financial General Bankshares despite warning signs, relying on representations by CCAH's shareholders and lawyers that the report says were untrue; that U.S. handling of BCCI was hampered by lack of coordination among the Federal Reserve, the FDIC and the OCC; and that although the Federal Reserve identified money laundering at BCCI's Miami office in 1987, it then lacked the power to order the closure of a state-chartered foreign bank.
facts.quote: hampered by lack of coordination among the regulators, which included the Federal Reserve, the FDIC, and the OCC

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: The Regulators

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) states that BCCI had no single regulator: its holding company and one of its major banking subsidiaries were chartered in Luxembourg but neither conducted banking business there, while BCCI managed most of its global business from offices in London; its other home, the Cayman Islands, did not regulate any bank licensed there. The New York District Attorney's staff concluded that this structure multiplied BCCI's opportunities to conceal fraud.
facts.quote: Both the holding company for BCCI and one of its major banking subsidiaries were chartered in Luxembourg, but neither conducted banking business in that country. Meanwhile, BCCI appears to manage most of its global business out of offices in London.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: The Regulators

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI and Law Enforcement - District Attorney of New York

facts.claim: On July 29, 1991, Manhattan District Attorney Robert Morgenthau announced a New York grand jury indictment of BCCI, its founder Agha Hasan Abedi, Swaleh Naqvi (the bank's chief operating officer until October 1990) and four affiliates, on charges including defrauding investors, falsifying records and stealing more than $30 million. Morgenthau described the case as 'the largest bank fraud in world financial history'. The Federal Reserve announced its own enforcement action against BCCI the same day.
facts.quote: the largest bank fraud in world financial history

sources.publisher: Tulsa World (Associated Press)
sources.title: NY Indicts BCCI, Founder; Fed Seeks $200 Million Fine

facts.claim: On July 29, 1991, the Federal Reserve Board announced formal enforcement proceedings against BCCI Holdings (Luxembourg) S.A. and related entities, including the assessment of a $200 million civil money penalty against BCCI and its related banks and companies and actions to bar individuals including Agha Hasan Abedi and Swaleh Naqvi from U.S. banking. The Board stated that BCCI owned Credit and Commerce American Holdings (CCAH), the parent of First American, in violation of the Bank Holding Company Act and had concealed its intended ownership and control of CCAH at the time of CCAH's 1980 application to acquire First American.
facts.quote: assessment of a $200 million civil money penalty against BCCI and its related banks and companies

sources.publisher: Federal Reserve Board
sources.title: Press release: enforcement proceedings against BCCI Holdings (Luxembourg) S.A. and related entities

facts.claim: A federal grand jury in Washington, D.C. indicted BCCI on November 15, 1991 on RICO charges. A plea agreement filed on December 19, 1991 provided for BCCI pleading guilty to charges brought by New York County District Attorney Robert M. Morgenthau and U.S. Attorney Jay B. Stephens and forfeiting its roughly $550 million of U.S. assets, which Attorney General William Barr called the largest single criminal payment in history. On January 24, 1992, Judge Joyce Hens Green of the U.S. District Court for D.C. accepted the guilty pleas of the four corporate defendants (United States v. BCCI Holdings (Luxembourg) S.A., Crim. No. 91-0655) and entered a forfeiture order under 18 U.S.C. § 1963.
facts.quote: On January 24, 1992, the court accepted the guilty pleas of the four corporate defendants and the plea agreement, then entered a forfeiture order under 18 U.S.C. § 1963.

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (hosted by vLex)
sources.title: U.S. v. BCCI Holdings (Luxembourg), S.A., Crim. Action No. 91-0655 (JHG)

sources.publisher: UPI
sources.title: BCCI forfeits all US assets

sources.publisher: UPI
sources.title: Judge accepts BCCI plea

facts.claim: UPI reported that, under the plea agreement accepted on January 24, 1992, approximately $100 million of the forfeited funds would be used to support BCCI's main American subsidiary, First American Bankshares Inc., $150 million would pay U.S. creditors, $275 million would pay foreign creditors and the remainder would pay civil fines and penalties in the United States. Judge Green said the settlement was in the public interest because it would allow depositors to recover some of their money and assure BCCI's cooperation in the prosecution of its founder and others; Attorney General Barr said charges against former executives including Agha Hasan Abedi and Swaleh Naqvi remained pending.
facts.quote: approximately $100 million of the funds would be used to prop up BCCI's main American subsidiary, First American Bankshares Inc., $150 million to go to pay U.S. creditors, $275 million to pay foreign creditors and the remainder to pay civil fines and penalties in the United States

sources.publisher: UPI
sources.title: Judge accepts BCCI plea

facts.claim: A chapter on BCCI in the IMF publication 'Current Legal Issues Affecting Central Banks, Volume IV' states that the Federal Reserve's charges against BCCI were resolved as part of a comprehensive plea agreement that also resolved the parallel criminal prosecutions by the U.S. Department of Justice and the New York County District Attorney; under it the Federal Reserve agreed to stay collection of its penalty in light of the asset forfeiture, and BCCI's interest in the First American banks was required to be fully divested, a requirement the chapter reports was met.
facts.quote: The Federal Reserve's charges were resolved as part of a comprehensive plea agreement that also resolved parallel criminal prosecutions against BCCI brought by the U.S. Department of Justice and the New York County District Attorney.

sources.publisher: International Monetary Fund
sources.title: Chapter 19: BCCI: The Lessons for Banking Supervision, in Current Legal Issues Affecting Central Banks, Volume IV

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) states that when BCCI was closed on July 5, 1991, the Abu Dhabi government, its ruling family and an investment company holding the family's assets were the official majority owners with 77 percent of the bank, and that because the remaining 23 percent was held by nominees and by BCCI's affiliate ICIC, Abu Dhabi was effectively the sole owner. The report records that Abu Dhabi shareholders bought 20 percent of BCCI at its founding in 1972 for $500,000, a stake that fell to just over one percent within three years.
facts.quote: the Abu Dhabi government, its ruling family, and an investment company holding the family's assets were the official majority owners with 77 percent

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Abu Dhabi: BCCI's Founding and Majority Shareholders

facts.claim: The Deseret News reported in August 1991 that Abu Dhabi's ruler, Sheikh Zayed, had invested more than $1 billion to rescue BCCI in 1989 and taken majority control in 1990, giving Abu Dhabi a 77.4 percent stake, and that after the closure Abu Dhabi began trying to recover about $2 billion in loans owed to BCCI.
facts.quote: Sheikh Zayed invested more than $1 billion to rescue the bank in 1989 and took majority control in 1990

sources.publisher: Deseret News
sources.title: Abu Dhabi starts trying to recover $2 billion in loans owed to BCCI

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) describes BCCI as a Luxembourg holding company, BCCI Holdings, above two banking subsidiaries: BCCI S.A. (Luxembourg; mostly European and Middle East locations) and BCCI Overseas (Grand Cayman; mostly Third World countries). Abedi split the annual audits between Ernst & Whinney (holding company and BCCI Luxembourg) and Price Waterhouse (BCCI Overseas) until Ernst & Whinney withdrew in 1986 and Price Waterhouse took on a consolidated audit in 1987. The report concluded this division between two auditors, neither able to audit all operations, was a significant mechanism by which BCCI hid its frauds in its early years.
facts.quote: BCCI's decision to divide its operations between two auditors, neither of whom had the right to audit all BCCI operations, was a significant mechanism by which BCCI was able to hide its frauds during its early years

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: The Origin and Early Years of BCCI

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Executive Summary

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) describes the Cayman Islands entities known collectively as ICIC as the principal 'bank within a bank' at BCCI. ICIC (Overseas) Limited was incorporated on April 6, 1976 as an offshore bank to facilitate the purchase and sale of BCCI shares and to provide private banking services for BCCI shareholders and customers; the report states that when Mohammed Hammoud's BCCI loans became delinquent they were simply transferred from BCCI to ICIC.
facts.quote: ICIC (Overseas) Limited, was incorporated on April 6, 1976 as an offshore bank to facilitate the purchase and sale of BCCI shares and to provide private banking services for BCCI shareholders and customers

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair (report index)

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Mohammed Hammoud: BCCI's Flexible Front-Man

facts.claim: The Bingham inquiry into the supervision of BCCI, commissioned by HM Treasury after the July 1991 closure, reported on 22 October 1992. It examined the Bank of England's supervision of BCCI under the Banking Acts and whether the UK authorities' action was appropriate and timely. Lord Justice Bingham found the Bank's supervision had been deficient in important respects, described the affair as 'a tragedy of errors, misunderstandings and failures of communications', and concluded that the conduct of Treasury ministers and officials was not open to criticism. It was not asked whether the Bank should bear financial responsibility or whether depositors should be compensated.
facts.quote: a tragedy of errors, misunderstandings and failures of communications

sources.publisher: UK Parliament (Hansard, House of Commons)
sources.title: BCCI (Bingham Report)

sources.publisher: UK Parliament (Hansard, House of Lords)
sources.title: BCCI: Bingham Report

facts.claim: An Early Day Motion tabled in the UK House of Commons in 2012 stated that the BCCI liquidation was drawing to a close after 21 years, that a 3.5% dividend was about to be paid, that the liquidators, Deloitte Touche, had set 17 May 2012 for the final creditors' meeting, and that creditors had received 90% of their money.
facts.quote: the liquidators, Deloitte Touche, had set 17 May 2012 for the final creditors' meeting

sources.publisher: UK Parliament (Early Day Motions)
sources.title: Bank of Credit and Commerce International - Close of Liquidation

facts.claim: A law-firm note published on Lexology states that ordinary creditors in the Cayman Islands, UK and Luxembourg pooling estates of BCCI were paid back 90 cents in the dollar after a 22-year liquidation, that the closure of the liquidations of BCCI S.A. and BCCI Holdings was decided by the Luxembourg Commercial Court on 5 July 2013, and that in 2016 the Luxembourg Court of Appeal refused a creditor's challenge to that order for lack of standing.
facts.quote: ordinary creditors in the Cayman Islands, UK and Luxembourg pooling estates were finally paid back 90 cents in the Dollar (90%) after a 22-year liquidation

sources.publisher: Lexology (law-firm article)
sources.title: BCCI case: The Luxembourg Court of Appeal refuses to reopen the liquidation proceedings

facts.claim: BCCI's Swiss affiliate, Banque de Commerce et de Placements in Geneva, was sold in July 1991; the Senate Foreign Relations Committee report states that when BCCI was closed, its Swiss affiliate was almost immediately sold to a Turkish banking group, Cukurova. Alfred Hartmann had been chairman of the Geneva bank until the sale.
facts.quote: when BCCI was closed, its Swiss affiliate was almost immediately sold to a Turkish banking group, Cukorova

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair (report index)

sources.publisher: Wikipedia
sources.title: Alfred Hartmann (banker)

facts.claim: A 1999 opinion of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia in the BCCI forfeiture proceedings (United States v. BCCI Holdings (Luxembourg) S.A., 69 F. Supp. 2d 36) describes an entity wholly owned by the ICIC Staff Benefit Trust for the benefit of BCCI employees, established by a gift of BCCI shares from ICIC Holdings.
facts.quote: wholly owned by the ICIC Staff Benefit Trust for the benefit of BCCI Employees, established by a gift of BCCI shares from ICIC Holdings

sources.publisher: U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia (hosted by Justia)
sources.title: United States v. BCCI Holdings, Luxembourg, S.A., 69 F. Supp. 2d 36 (D.D.C. 1999)

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) describes Price Waterhouse's June 1991 'Sandstorm' findings: the firm investigated some $600 million of BCCI deposits not recorded in BCCI's books and found that from 1977 to 1985 BCCI's treasury operations made significant losses that were concealed while significant profits were manufactured, the loans and fictitious profits put at roughly $600-700 million before funding costs. Techniques included misappropriating deposits without depositors' knowledge to adjust non-performing and bogus loan accounts and treasury losses, and creating loans with no commercial substance in the names of people without their knowledge.
facts.quote: Price Waterhouse investigated some $600 million of BCCI deposits not recorded in BCCI's books / over the period from 1977 to 1985, the Treasury operations of Sandstorm made significant losses. These losses were concealed and at the same time significant profits were manufactured / misappropriation of deposits without depositors knowledge to provide funds to adjust non-performing and bogus loan accounts, and Treasury losses

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI and its Accountants

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) summarizes Price Waterhouse's findings on BCCI as concealed treasury losses, failure to record deposits and other liabilities, fictitious loan accounts, the use of funds from ICIC (which BCCI controlled), circular routing of funds and collusion with customers over false confirmations, and records that Price Waterhouse later wrote that with hindsight the practices appeared a deliberate way to fictitiously inflate income.
facts.quote: concealed Treasury losses, failure to record deposits and other liabilities; the creation of fictitious loan accounts; the use of funds from ICIC which were controlled by BCCI, circular routing of funds, and collusion with customers over false confirmations / with the benefit of hindsight, it appears more sinister in that it now seems to have been a deliberate way to fictitiously inflate income

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI and its Accountants

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) records that an April 1990 Price Waterhouse report to the Bank of England called a number of BCCI transactions 'false and deceitful' and said it was impossible at that time to determine how far the fraud reached, and that Price Waterhouse's June 22, 1991 draft Section 41 report found that fraud on a significant scale had been committed, involving a significant number of people both inside and outside the bank.
facts.quote: false and deceitful / it was impossible at the present time to determine just how far the fraud reached / fraud on a significant scale had been committed and that it had involved a significant number of people both inside and outside the bank

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI and its Accountants

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) concluded that the auditing process failed to work in BCCI's case, and that Price Waterhouse's UK partnership knew of gross irregularities in BCCI's handling of loans to CCAH/First American and was told of violations of U.S. banking laws by BCCI and its borrowers in connection with CCAH/First American, but failed to advise the partners of its U.S. affiliate or any U.S. regulator.
facts.quote: the UK partnership knew of gross irregularities in BCCI's handling of loans to CCAH/First American and was told of violations of U.S. banking laws by BCCI and its borrowers in connection with CCAH/First American, and failed to advise the partners of its U.S. affiliate or any U.S. regulator

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI and its Accountants

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) records that on July 29, 1991 the New York District Attorney indicted BCCI, citing the case as People v. BCCI, and found that Justice Department personnel in Washington, Miami and Tampa obstructed and impeded attempts by District Attorney Robert Morgenthau to obtain critical information concerning BCCI in 1989, 1990 and 1991. The report states that it was not the regulatory process itself that brought about the exposure and removal of BCCI in the United States or the United Kingdom, and that the district attorney's criminal investigation prompted the final regulatory action.
facts.quote: On July 29, 1991, the New York District Attorney indicted BCCI. / Justice Department personnel in Washington, Miami and Tampa obstructed and impeded attempts by New York District Attorney Robert Morgenthau to obtain critical information concerning BCCI in 1989, 1990, and 1991.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI and Law Enforcement - District Attorney of New York

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Executive Summary

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) records that former Customs Commissioner William von Raab told the Subcommittee that Customs agents handling the C-Chase investigation of BCCI had discovered several BCCI accounts that were actually accounts held by the CIA and were told to cease investigating those accounts; the report notes that an Assistant U.S. Attorney denied ever finding CIA involvement and an Assistant Attorney General said no one from the CIA had tried to interfere with the case.
facts.quote: had discovered in the course of their work several BCCI accounts that were actually accounts held by the CIA

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI, the CIA and Foreign Intelligence

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) records that Acting CIA Director Richard Kerr, testifying in October 1991, acknowledged that the CIA had made extensive use of First American, BCCI's secretly held U.S. subsidiary, for a variety of purposes including ordinary banking and savings accounts, and said the agency had given the Treasury Department information about BCCI's secret ownership of First American in 1985.
facts.quote: the CIA had made extensive use of First American for a variety of purposes, including for ordinary banking and savings accounts

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: BCCI, the CIA and Foreign Intelligence

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) states that after fraud was found in 1990 the Abu Dhabi government agreed to formally buy BCCI, assert control and guarantee its losses, and that a Price Waterhouse note in BCCI's annual report described the government as having subscribed US$400 million for new shares and holding over 77 percent of the bank.

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Abu Dhabi: BCCI's Founding and Majority Shareholders

facts.claim: The Senate Foreign Relations Committee report (December 1992) found that members of Abu Dhabi's ruling family appear to have contributed no more than $500,000 to BCCI's capitalization before April 1990 despite owning almost a quarter of the shares, that Price Waterhouse specifically found they acquired their shares on the basis of guaranteed rates of return and buy-back arrangements, and that the Abu Dhabi Investment Authority's 10 percent stake from 1980 appeared to be genuine.
facts.quote: members of Abu Dhabi's ruling family appear to have contributed no more than $500,000 to BCCI's capitalization prior to April 1990, despite owning almost a quarter of the shares / Price Waterhouse specifically found that members of the Ruling Family of Abu Dhabi acquired their shares on the basis of guaranteed rates of return and buy-back arrangements

sources.publisher: U.S. Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (hosted by Federation of American Scientists)
sources.title: The BCCI Affair: Abu Dhabi: BCCI's Founding and Majority Shareholders

facts.claim: On June 14, 1994 a court in the United Arab Emirates sentenced 12 former BCCI executives to a total of 56 years in prison; UPI reported that founder Agha Hasan Abedi and treasurer Ziauddin Ali Akbar were tried and convicted in absentia, with Abedi sentenced to six years, and that Swaleh Naqvi received four sentences totaling 11 years on nine counts. Naqvi was later transferred to U.S. custody; the Washington Post reported in June 1994 that he had agreed to plead guilty and on October 20, 1994 that Judge Joyce Hens Green sentenced him to 11 years, of which he was required to serve eight after the court credited the three years he had spent in UAE and U.S. custody.
facts.quote: The bank's founder, Agha Hassan Abedi, and treasurer, Ziauddin Ali Akbar, were tried and convicted in absentia. / Naqvi, 59, a British citizen, received four sentences totaling 11 years for the nine counts he faced. / required to serve only eight years of the sentence after Green took into account the three years he spent in custody of UAE and U.S. authorities

sources.publisher: UPI
sources.title: UAE jails and fines BCCI executives

sources.publisher: Washington Post
sources.title: Former BCCI Executive Agrees to Plead Guilty

sources.publisher: Washington Post
sources.title: Former BCCI Official Naqvi Sentenced to Prison

facts.claim: MEED reported that BCCI's liquidators, Deloitte, paid a first dividend of about 24.5 percent in December 1996, calculated on US$2.65 billion of free funds against claims estimated at US$10.6 billion; that by late 1997 some $4,500 million, or 46 percent of funds lost, had been returned in two dividends; and that a third dividend of about 14 percent would bring the total to 60 percent of claims. A 1999 D.C. federal district court opinion likewise recorded 46 percent repaid on admitted claims in two dividends. Accountancy Daily reported in 2005 that a further 6 percent dividend brought the total paid to 81 percent, against 10 percent envisaged at the outset in 1993.
facts.quote: first dividend of about 24.5% in December 1996, calculated on the basis of there being US$2.65 billion of free funds payable to a creditor population estimated at US$10.6 billion / returned some $4,500 million, or 46 per cent of funds lost, in two dividend payments / a total of 60 per cent of claims made by creditors will have been met

sources.publisher: MEED
sources.title: BCCI creditors finally get their first pay-out

sources.publisher: MEED

openQuestions: Unsupported by any source found: the owner's draft claims BCCI's 'operational infrastructure and personnel migrated directly into Swiss private-banking secrecy desks, Cayman Islands trust structures and Liechtenstein anstalts'. A search for former BCCI staff or structures moving to Swiss private banks, Cayman trust companies or Liechtenstein entities returned nothing stating such a migration. What sources do give: BCCI's own subsidiaries were chartered in Luxembourg (BCCI Holdings, BCCI S.A.) and the Cayman Islands (BCCI Overseas, ICIC); its Geneva affiliate Banque de Commerce et de Placements was sold in July 1991 (to the Turkish group Cukurova, per the Senate report); the estates were wound up by Deloitte over 21-22 years. Nothing found on Liechtenstein.

Country count: the owner's draft says 78 countries; the Senate report's executive summary (already in the approved summary) says 73. Other sources give other figures. Verify before using either number.

'Dual-ledger system of unrecorded deposits': the Senate report's account of Price Waterhouse's findings (some $600 million of deposits not recorded in BCCI's books; concealed treasury losses and manufactured profits; fictitious loan accounts; ICIC funds; circular routing; false confirmations) is now recorded from chapter 10. Secondary accounts (AccountingWEB, https://www.accountingweb.co.uk/breakthrough-for-bcci-sandstorm-report-foi-request ; Financial Transparency Coalition) say the UK released most of the Sandstorm Report on 7 September 2011 after a freedom-of-information case; the released text itself was not retrieved.

'Key insiders, intelligence cutouts and Gulf royals pulled out their capital before the freeze': no source found. The sources found show Abu Dhabi as 77% owner at closure after investing more than $1 billion in 1989-90 (Senate report ch. 14; Deseret News 1991-08-03). The Washington Post reported on 1992-05-14 that Abu Dhabi was said to block access to data and witnesses in BCCI probes (https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/business/1992/05/14/abu-dhabi-said-to-block-access-to-data-witnesses-in-bcci-probes/5daf3320-948b-45df-a872-f09112fccf81/ ; no passage retrieved). Wikipedia states Abu Dhabi shareholders agreed a $1.8 billion compensation package for creditors in 1994 (unverified).

'CIA black-budget financing for the Afghan mujahideen' and 'covert arms-trafficking receipts' via BCCI: the searches this session covered the CIA's accounts at and use of BCCI (Senate report ch. 11) but did not retrieve passages on Afghan financing specifically. The approved summary already notes the report documented support of arms trafficking. Iran-Contra and Latin American cartel links were not searched (search budget exhausted).

Seven-country closure count: only a bookseller's description says offices were shut in the UK, the US and five other countries on 5 July 1991; the Bank of England report names only the UK, Luxembourg and Grand Cayman plus unnamed 'other jurisdictions'.

Creditor recovery: the 2012 Early Day Motion and a Lexology note give about 90%; Wikipedia says Deloitte claimed about 75% by 2013; a MEED piece (https://www.meed.com/big-bills-still-to-be-paid/) is said to report 81% paid by around 2005 against 10% expected at the outset in 1993. The figures depend on which estates and claim bases are counted.

Creditor recovery: the dividend history is now recorded (24.5% first dividend December 1996; 46% after two dividends by late 1997 and per the 1999 D.D.C. opinion; 60% after the third; 81% after a 6% dividend in 2005 per Accountancy Daily); the 2012 Early Day Motion and a Lexology note give about 90% at the close. A liquidators' notice or court order stating the final dividend and date was not found in two searches (Deloitte's site and thegazette.co.uk returned nothing; independent.co.uk, telegraph.co.uk and bbc.com block the search crawler). A BCCI history site, https://bccibank-insights.com/key-events/1991-onwards-liquidation , hosts the English liquidators' reports and states that creditors of the principal estates recovered more than 90% of admitted claims and Hong Kong creditors were repaid in full; its publisher is unidentified and it is not cited. Wikipedia's '75% by 2013' figure conflicts with the above.

Page attribution within the Senate report: two facts cite the report index page because the search results did not say which chapter holds the passage (ICIC incorporation; the sale of the Swiss affiliate to Cukurova). The 'heavily censored' Sandstorm passage and the 'tragedy of errors' Bingham quote should also be checked against the cited pages during review.

Entity index: neither 'bcci' nor 'federal-reserve' is an id in public/data/entities.json even though approved findings files exist under those ids; connections here use those ids with toName/toType filled.

Chapter attribution within the Senate report: the Sandstorm passages and the auditor finding are cited to chapter 10 (BCCI and its Accountants) because that chapter was among the pages returned and the subject matches, but the search extract did not say which page holds each sentence; chapter 4 (BCCI's Criminality, https://irp.fas.org/congress/1992_rpt/bcci/04crime.htm ) was returned alongside it. The 'obstructed and impeded' finding and the 'not the regulatory process itself' sentence are cited to chapters 9 and 1 on the same basis (chapter 12, The Regulators, may hold the latter). Check during review.

The Senate report's footnotes cite 'People vs. BCCI, July 29, 1991' and 'People vs. Abedi, July 29, 1992', while another footnote gives July 29, 1991 for People v. Abedi; the dates are inconsistent within the report. The AP report already cited gives July 29, 1991 for the indictment naming Abedi and Naqvi.

UAE sentences: UPI (June 14, 1994) gives six years for Abedi and 11 years for Naqvi and counts 12 executives; a later UPI report counts 13 executives and gives Naqvi 14 years in absentia; UPI (January 31, 1995, https://www.upi.com/Archives/1995/01/31/Abu-Dhabi-to-buy-BCCI-share-in-UAE-bank/6991791528400/ ) gives Abedi a nine-year sentence; the Deseret News obituary gives eight years. Only the June 14, 1994 figures are recorded in the fact.

The Abu Dhabi chapter gives both 'over 77 percent' and 'over 78 percent' for the ruling family's post-1990 holding, and records Sheikh Zayed's personal stake at 20 percent in 1972 and 4.11 percent after buying 80,000 shares in 1980; the Deseret News figure of 77.4 percent is a third variant.
